issues.legal_issue: Whether a transfer expressed as a sale with a condition for repayment is a mortgage by conditional sale or an outright sale with a right to repurchase.
material_facts: The owners executed one deed that used sale language, described the transferee as becoming proprietor, and provided for the owners to regain possession if they repaid within a specified time; if they did not, the transferee would remain in possession and take the produce.
The deed did not expressly provide for reconveyance of title, and its language was ambiguous when read as a whole.
Most of the stated consideration discharged an existing mortgage debt, and additional money was advanced to continue proceedings concerning the land, which benefited the owners if successful.

The transferee was to possess the property and retain its produce, and the deed contained provisions requiring the owners to repay the consideration with interest and damages if the transferee was dispossessed.
The plaintiff sought redemption on the basis that the deed created a mortgage, and the courts below had reached conflicting conclusions about the deed's character.
issues.conclusion: The deed was a mortgage by conditional sale, so the appeal was allowed and the lower appellate court's decree was restored, apart from costs.
issues.legal_principle: The parties' intention controls, but it is first determined from the document. Clear language governs without extrinsic inquiry; surrounding circumstances may be considered when the document is ambiguous. Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, as amended, a sale and repurchase agreement in separate documents cannot constitute a mortgage, while a single document does not automatically constitute either a mortgage or a sale. Where one document has the form of an ostensible sale and its conditions satisfy section 58(c), it is to be construed as a mortgage unless express words indicate otherwise or, in an ambiguous case, the surrounding circumstances necessarily point to the contrary. The Court relied on Balkishen Das v. Legge, Alderson v. White, Bhagwan Sahai v. Bhagwan Din, and Jhanda Singh v. Wahid-ud-din.

rule.if: redemption_suit_over_disputed_transfer and single_transfer_document and ostensible_sale_language and repayment_condition_returns_possession and nonpayment_leaves_transferee_in_possession and ambiguous_document and no_express_words_negating_mortgage and existing_debt_and_property_benefit_proceedings

predicates.redemption_suit_over_disputed_transfer: A claimant brought a suit seeking redemption based on the assertion that a disputed transfer created a mortgage.
predicates.single_transfer_document: The parties embodied the transfer and its repayment condition in one document.
predicates.ostensible_sale_language: The document used language presenting the transaction as a sale and the transferee as the owner.
predicates.repayment_condition_returns_possession: The document provided that repayment within the stated time would return possession to the transferors.
predicates.nonpayment_leaves_transferee_in_possessi: The document provided that failure to repay would leave the transferee in possession and entitled to the property's produce.
predicates.ambiguous_document: The document's language, read as a whole, did not clearly resolve whether the transaction was a mortgage or an outright sale.
predicates.no_express_words_negating_mortgage: The document contained no express statement that the transaction was not a mortgage.
predicates.existing_debt_and_property_benefit_proce: Most of the consideration discharged an existing debt, and additional money was advanced for proceedings concerning the property that could benefit the transferors.

issues.definition: When a redemption suit concerns a single, ambiguous transfer document framed as a sale, its repayment conditions and surrounding facts support treating the transaction as a mortgage by conditional sale if no express words negate that characterization.
